name: Escalator — the contract price-increase agent for recurring-service contractors
one_liner: For the controller or owner at a $3M-$50M commercial janitorial, landscaping, security-guard or fire-protection contractor, Escalator reads the signed customer agreements, finds every annual escalator, CPI clause, wage pass-through and notice deadline, checks them against what was actually invoiced in QuickBooks/Aspire/ServiceTitan, and produces a dated calendar of increases due plus the ready-to-send notice letter for each one.
problem: Commercial recurring-service contractors (janitorial, landscaping maintenance, guard services, fire/life-safety inspection, elevator) run on hundreds of multi-year site agreements. Most of those agreements contain a price-adjustment right: a fixed annual uplift, a CPI-linked adjustment (often capped), a change-in-law/minimum-wage pass-through, or a renewal repricing window — usually with a notice requirement (30/60/90 days before the anniversary). The clause lives in a signed PDF in a shared drive or an email thread; the billing lives in QuickBooks or an ops platform (Aspire, ServiceTitan, BuildOps, ServiceTrade). Nothing connects them. The anniversary passes, nobody sends the notice, and the account is billed at the old rate for another year — permanently, because next year's increase compounds off the un-raised base. On a $120k/yr contract a missed 3% uplift is $3,600 in year one and roughly $11.1k cumulative over three years (arithmetic, our calculation); a 150-contract book with even 20% of escalators missed is a six-figure annual gross-margin hole, at ~100% incremental margin. Today the workaround is a spreadsheet maintained by one contract administrator, or nothing at all. Our research found that Aspire, ServiceTitan, BuildOps, ServiceTrade and Inspect Point all support recurring agreements and bulk manual price changes, but none publicly documents reading a CPI clause, computing the indexed rate with cap/floor and base month, and pushing it into recurring billing with a notice deadline (Perplexity review of vendor docs and user reviews).
target_customer: Buyer: the owner/CFO/controller at a US commercial service contractor doing $3M-$50M revenue with 50-400 recurring site agreements — commercial cleaning (63,999 US employer firms in 2022), landscape maintenance (114,570 firms), guard services, fire protection, elevator. Second buyer, higher value: the operating partner / CFO at a PE-backed facility-services roll-up platform (Pye-Barker, Summit Fire & Security, Landscape Workshop, Sizemore and others were active acquirers in 2026), who wants escalator realization measured across every add-on's contract book at close and every year after.
why_now: Three things changed in the last year. (1) Document models got good enough to read a 14-page janitorial MSA and extract the escalation clause, its index, base month, cap/floor, cap-on-notice and anniversary with citations — this is exactly a16z's "startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" Big Idea (Jennifer Li, https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-1/) and Sarah Wang's "systems of record lose ground" (same link): the value moves from storing the contract to acting on it. (2) A hard, dated cost shock: 16 states raise their minimum wage on 1 Jan 2027, from +$0.26 in Nebraska to +$1.27 in Michigan (EPI, Ballotpedia), landing squarely on the most labour-intensive contract books in America — contractors must either pass it through or eat it, and the pass-through right only works if someone finds the clause and sends the notice in time. On federal SCA work, FAR 52.222-43 requires the contractor to notify the CO within 30 days of receiving a new wage determination or risk the adjustment. (3) The a16z "forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" idea (Joe Schmidt, https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-2/) describes exactly this buyer: a non-Silicon-Valley operator who will never configure a platform but will pay for a delivered outcome. And the SpaceXSI/Grok accounting-bot post that seeded tonight's thinking shows the pattern: a bot that owns one narrow order-to-cash step end to end and escalates judgment calls.
comparables: Halo (myhalo.ai) — closest direct comparable found: emails you a report comparing a 24-month QuickBooks "Sales by Customer Detail" export against your contracts to flag unsigned customers, missed escalators and upcoming renewals, aimed at landscaping/janitorial/security/HVAC. Gap: it is free-for-now, manual/service-assisted (email your export, results in a week), no QuickBooks or ops-platform integration, no ongoing enforcement, no CPI maths. Validates the problem; leaves the product open. • Revomo (revomo.ai) — "Contract Pricing & Renewals" compares invoices to agreed prices and tracks renewal/notice deadlines; $18k/yr platform + $18-36k per capability, sold to PE portfolios, and the contract module is explicitly in alpha with design partners. Gap: enterprise price and config-led, not for a 150-contract janitorial firm. • RevSync MSP (revsyncmsp.com, $299-1,200/mo + 15% of recovered revenue) and Leakage Finder (CA$49-149/mo) — same economic model (find leakage, charge for recovery) but only for MSPs reconciling vendor billing to PSA; neither touches signed customer contracts or escalator clauses. • Aspire, ServiceTitan, BuildOps, ServiceTrade, Inspect Point — systems of record for these trades; all support recurring agreements, renewal flags and bulk manual percentage/dollar price changes, but our review of their docs and reviews found no documented automatic CPI-clause interpretation (index, base month, cap/floor), no notice-deadline enforcement, and Aspire users complain about rigid editing and weak reporting. • ContractSafe ($450+/mo) and general CLMs — store contracts and remind on dates, but do not compare the clause to the invoice. • Lease-administration firms (ReboLease, KriyaGo) — prove buyers already pay humans to audit escalations, but on the real-estate side and as a service, not software.
market_note: Estimate, stated as such. US commercial cleaning: ~64,000 employer firms; landscaping: ~115,000 (Census-derived figures cited by industry summaries). If 8% of those two categories alone sit in the $3M-$50M band with a real contract book, that is roughly 14,000 target firms, before guard, fire-protection and elevator. Willingness to pay is anchored by real comparables we found: RevSync (MSP billing reconciliation) charges $299-$1,200/mo plus 15% of recovered revenue; Leakage Finder CA$49-149/mo; Stratgik sells a $15,000 revenue-leakage pilot with ongoing service from $4,000/mo; Revomo lists $18,000/yr platform plus $18-36k per capability for PE portfolios. A $500-$1,500/mo subscription plus a success fee on year-one recovered increases is therefore inside an established price band. A 150-contract book with ~$15M revenue and 20% of escalators missed plausibly recovers $100k+ at near-100% margin, so a $12k/yr price is a <15% take. The PE-platform motion (one platform, 10-40 add-ons) is the path from $1k/mo deals to six-figure ACVs.
risks: 1) The clause may not be there. If a large share of SMB contractor agreements have no escalation or change-in-law language at all, the product degrades from "collect what you're owed" to "help me ask for a raise" — a much softer sell. Our research could not find prevalence data; this is the first thing to measure. 2) Collection risk, not detection risk. Finding a missed escalator is not the same as getting the customer to pay it; if acceptance rates are low or the contractor fears losing the account, the ROI story collapses. We found no reliable acceptance-rate benchmark (one trade source claims 60-75%, undocumented). 3) Incumbent absorption: Aspire/ServiceTitan/BuildOps already hold the agreement record and could ship escalator automation as a feature; the defence is being multi-system, contract-PDF-first, and sold as an outcome with a success fee.
riskiest_assumptions: Most fragile first: (1) that a meaningful share — call it 40%+ — of these contractors' signed agreements actually contain an enforceable escalation, CPI or change-in-law clause, and that a meaningful share of those went unapplied last year. Everything rests on this and we found no data; it is answerable in a week by reading 20 real contracts. (2) That the owner/controller will hand over signed PDFs and a QuickBooks sales export to a stranger — Halo's free offer exists precisely because this trust barrier is real. (3) That customers accept the retro/forward increase often enough that the recovered dollars dwarf the fee; if acceptance is below ~50%, the success-fee model breaks and it becomes a flat SaaS sale against a crowded ops-platform budget.
first_customers: Ten named-type buyers, all reachable this month: (1-4) owners of $5-20M commercial janitorial firms in California, Michigan, Washington and New Jersey — four of the 16 states with a 1 Jan 2027 minimum-wage increase, so the cost shock is dated and specific; find them via BSCAI and ISSA member directories and local BSCAI chapter meetings. (5-6) commercial landscape maintenance firms from the NALP member list and the Landscape Management LM150 tail (the $5-30M names, not the top 25). (7-8) fire/life-safety inspection contractors from the NFSA/AFSA member lists running ServiceTrade or Inspect Point. (9-10) the operating partner at one PE-backed facility-services platform doing add-ons (Landscape Workshop, Sizemore, Summit Fire & Security are publicly active 2026 acquirers) — pitch the contract-book audit at close. Cold outreach line: "send me 20 of your signed agreements and your 2025-26 sales-by-customer export; I'll tell you free which increases you were entitled to and did not bill."
validation_test: This week, run the Halo play but better and paid-intent-tested. Get 5 contractors (BSCAI/NALP directories, LinkedIn DMs to owners, plus one PE operating partner) to send 20 signed agreements each plus a 24-month QuickBooks "Sales by Customer Detail" export. Hand-process with a model: extract clause type, index, cap, anniversary, notice window; compare the billed rate trajectory per customer; produce a one-page "increases you were entitled to and did not bill" with a dollar total and a draft notice letter for the top three. PASS if (a) across the 100 contracts at least 35 contain a price-adjustment right, (b) at least 2 of the 5 contractors show $25k+ of unapplied increases, and (c) at least 2 of them say yes to "$1,000/month plus 10% of what we recover in year one, starting with your whole book" — a verbal yes plus a signed LOI counts, a "send me info" does not. FAIL if clauses are rare or every owner says "we just renegotiate at renewal, we don't use the clause."
build_plan: Stack the builder already has: TypeScript, a document-capable model API (Claude/Gemini for long PDF extraction with citations), a simple Next.js app, and UiPath/agent orchestration for the recurring watch job. Narrowest first version, sellable in weeks: (1) Ingest — drag-and-drop a folder of signed agreement PDFs plus a QuickBooks "Sales by Customer Detail" CSV (no QBO OAuth yet; the export is what Halo already proves customers will send). (2) Extract — per contract, a model pass returns a structured clause record: customer, site, annual value, adjustment type (fixed % / CPI-linked / change-in-law / renewal-only / none), index series and base month, cap and floor, anniversary date, notice days, auto-renewal terms — each field with the quoted source sentence and page number so the controller can verify in one click. (3) Compute — pull the real CPI-U series (BLS public API, free) and compute the rate that should be in force today; compare with the actual invoiced trajectory from the CSV; output "increases due, increases missed, dollars left on the table, compounding effect over 3 years". (4) Act — a dated calendar of the next 12 months of anniversaries and notice deadlines, and for each one a drafted customer notice letter quoting the clause and showing the maths. (5) Watch — a weekly agent re-checks the calendar and emails the controller 15 days before each notice deadline, escalating only exceptions. Cut for v1: QuickBooks/Aspire/ServiceTitan write-back (read-only CSV + copy-paste letter is enough to get paid), e-signature, SCA/FAR wage-determination module, multi-entity PE roll-up dashboards, any customer-facing portal. Sell it as a $2,500 fixed-fee first audit that converts to $1,000/mo + success fee.
reasoning: The night's strongest raw material was not the loudest bookmark (Claude Meetings, 81k likes) but the xAI accounting-bot post: a serious company describing bots that each own one narrow order-to-cash step end to end and escalate only judgment calls. The obvious move — build that for SMBs — is a graveyard (HighRadius, Tabs, Fazeshift, Monk, plus my own past Shiftlog). So I kept the shape and moved it to a buyer the AR-agent wave has entirely skipped: the commercial service contractor whose revenue is a book of multi-year site agreements. The step I chose is the most boring and most valuable one in that book — the annual price adjustment — because it is pure margin, it compounds forever when missed, and it is the one step every system of record in those trades declines to automate. Research confirmed the systems (Aspire, ServiceTitan, BuildOps, ServiceTrade, Inspect Point) do bulk manual percentage changes but not clause interpretation, notice enforcement or invoice reconciliation; the one direct comparable, myhalo.ai, is doing it by email, by hand, for free — the clearest possible signal that the problem is real and the product has not been built. The timing is not a vibe: 16 states raise minimum wage on 1 January 2027, and FAR 52.222-43 gives federal service contractors 30 days to claim a wage-determination adjustment. It beat the lease-escalation twin (crowded by MRI and a mature audit-services industry) and the SCA-only version (too narrow, slow sales) by having the widest underserved book with the fastest path to a first paid audit. Signals weighed: a16z's "startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" and "systems of record lose ground" (Part 1) gave the capability thesis, "forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" (Part 2) gave the go-to-market shape; YC's "AI for City Hall" and "Plaid for Government Benefits" were tempting but led to 12-18 month public-sector cycles for this one builder. I held the score at 8.1 rather than higher because the single thing that would make this a 9 — hard prevalence data on how many of these contracts carry an enforceable escalator and how many went unapplied — does not exist publicly, which is precisely what the week-one validation test is designed to settle. Fit for this builder is good: document extraction plus a scheduled watch agent plus drafted letters is squarely TypeScript-and-model-API work with a UiPath-style recurring job, and the first audit is a deliverable, not a platform. It does not repeat any library idea: Qualifile serves a contractor's compliance coordinator on prequal portals; Shortfall audits insurance commission statements for agencies; Declined handles insurance renewal conversations. None touches the service contractor's own customer-contract price-adjustment rights.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Escalator — contract price-escalation agent for commercial recurring-service contractors (janitorial/landscape/fire/guard). PICK. Named buyer, recurring annual money, dated 2027 wage forcing event, one near-identical comparable that is free and manual.
2. Grok-bot-for-SMB-order-to-cash — a packaged "five bots" accounting crew for 50-300 person companies, mirroring the SpaceXSI post. Dropped at screen: HighRadius, Tabs, Fazeshift, Monk, Growfin and a dozen funded AR agents already sell this exact workflow to this exact buyer; also overlaps past idea Shiftlog.
3. Bot HR / agent performance reviews — onboarding, scope, scorecards and "performance reviews" for AI coworkers, from the "we manage them like human teammates" line. Dropped: direct repeat of past ideas Shiftlog and Roster, and the governance angle is already crowded.
4. Implementation partner co-pilot for small Dynamics/NetSuite SIs — dropped as a repeat of past ideas Asbuilt and Conversion, and Auctor just raised $20M from Sequoia for the adjacent slice.
5. Agent approval inbox for non-developers — Cuttlefish-for-ops: one mobile queue where finance/ops staff approve agent actions. Finalist, then dropped: every orchestration platform (Copilot Studio, Zip, Lindy, Mastra, Sim) ships human-in-the-loop approvals natively; no standalone budget, and close to past idea Doublecheck.
6. Remote agent fleet control plane (from the @KlausCodes "any open source tool to control all my agents" ask) — dropped at screen: DigitalOcean Managed Agents + Cuttlefish, plus a dozen OSS projects, already occupy it, and the buyer is a developer with no budget.
7. Plaid-for-government-benefits wedge: a document-proof vault for FQHC/community-clinic patients re-proving income at renewal. Dropped: strong YC signal but 12-18 month public-sector sales cycle, and adjacent to past idea Frailty.
8. Lease-escalation audit for small commercial landlords and tenants — the same mechanic in CRE. Finalist, then dropped: MRI, ReboLease, KriyaGo and a mature lease-audit service industry already serve it; the contractor side is the same mechanic with no incumbents.
9. SCA / FAR 52.222-43 wage-determination claim agent for small federal service contractors. Finalist, folded into Escalator as a v2 module rather than a standalone: real 30-day deadline and real money, but the buyer universe is narrow and government sales cycles are slow — better as an upsell to a book we already hold.
10. Daily-SIP-style friction-removal fintech for an under-served market (from the Sipse bookmark) — dropped at generation: consumer fintech, regulated, needs distribution and capital this builder does not have, and no B2B agent edge.
11. Sub-$50 micro-investing / wealth-management-for-all wrapper on the a16z signal — dropped: same reasons as 10, plus the signal names incumbents already scaling.

PROJECT
1. Bottleneck — paste your week's tasks, get per-task RL-trainability with the named reason an agent can't learn it, weekly card. PICK: new May-2026 task-level dataset, first-person, repeatable, no direct prior art.
2. Roster-for-your-week (bot org chart from the SpaceXSI five-bot post) — DROPPED as a repeat: "Roster" (2026-11-19) already turns a job title into a named team of bots from O*NET tasks. Same audience, same workflow.
3. Agent fleet console — open-source dashboard to see/control agents on a remote laptop, from @KlausCodes' question. Dropped at screen: crowded field (paperclip, Cezar, awesome-agent-orchestrators lists nine+), needs a real backend, not a weekend static toy.
4. Untangle-score — paste a repo, get a code-smell card (leaky abstractions, copy-paste). Dropped at screen: jscpd/super-linter/SonarCloud cover it, and it's a thin variation on a tool named in a bookmark (@mazeincoding's /untangle-codebase) — explicitly off-limits.
5. Mac container migration check — drop a docker-compose.yml, see what works on Apple `container` 1.7.1 with its new local Kubernetes clusters. Finalist, lost: audience is small (Apple-silicon devs only), the output is a compatibility table nobody posts, and verifying real compatibility rules is a research project, not a weekend.
6. Geofence reminder builder — type "remind me 30 min after I get home if laundry is >5 days old", get an importable iOS Shortcut, from @trq212's post. Finalist, lost: no clean way to generate a valid, installable Shortcut file from a static page; output is private, nothing to share; freshness low (Shortcuts geofences are years old).
7. Meeting-to-whiteboard — paste a transcript, get the diagram Claude Meetings would have drawn. Dropped at screen: no Claude Meetings API, and the market is saturated (Miro/FigJam/MockFlow AI canvases, Claude artifacts themselves).
8. Demo-photo generator — riff on Auctor's "dog photo that booked hundreds of demos". Dropped at generate: pure gimmick, no return visit, and it reduces to another image-gen wrapper.
9. Country automation map — Global Automation Atlas (124 countries × 18,797 tasks) as a browsable map. Finalist, lost to Bottleneck: beautiful public data but third-person — you look at a country, not at yourself — and the Atlas already ships its own public explorer at automationatlas.org.
10. Investing-friction stripper (from @misbahspeaks' sipse post) — one input, plain-English fund jargon decoder. Dropped at generate: regulated territory, India-specific data access unverified, and the builder's profile points away from consumer fintech.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3 of 3): summarised the xAI Grok accounting-bot page (five bots, each owning one order-to-cash step, ~3-week onboarding, escalate on judgment — this became the structural template), Auctor (confirmed $20M Sequoia Series A and that it sells to system integrators, which killed candidate 4 and ruled out the implementation lane), and DigitalOcean Cuttlefish (confirmed the mobile approve-button space is already occupied by the infra vendors, killing candidates 5 and 6). A fourth summary on Sipse confirmed it is a Jar-team regular-plan MF distributor — consumer fintech, out of scope for this builder.
Screening pot (6 of 6): AR/order-to-cash agent landscape (crowded — HighRadius, Tabs, Monk, Fazeshift, Growfin); ERP-implementation AI tooling (crowded, Auctor funded); "manage AI agents like employees" (crowded + repeats past ideas); agent approval inboxes (native feature everywhere); SaaS provisioning/entitlement drift (no clean buyer); contract-to-billing leakage generally (crowded in SaaS). Net effect: five of six candidates died at screen, which pushed me out of the software-buyer lane entirely and into trades.
Deep research pot (12 of 12): revenue-leakage benchmarks and the SaaS incumbent set (Tabs, Fazeshift, Nue, Subscript) — all inconsistent and crowded, so I pivoted the buyer; MSP/service-contractor billing reconciliation (found RevSync $299-1,200/mo + 15% of recovered revenue, Leakage Finder CA$49-149/mo, Stratgik $15k pilot + $4k/mo — these set the price anchor); CRE lease escalation (found the ReboLease/KriyaGo/MRI audit industry, which killed the lease candidate but proved people pay humans for this mechanic); escalator prevalence in service contracts (no data — logged as the riskiest assumption); myhalo.ai (the key find: a free, manual, email-a-QuickBooks-export version of exactly this, with no integration); Aspire/ServiceTitan/BuildOps escalator capability (manual bulk changes only, no CPI logic — the gap); fire-protection/elevator platforms ServiceTrade and Inspect Point (same conclusion); market sizing (64k janitorial and 115k landscaping employer firms, no clean $2-50M band count); 2026-27 minimum-wage dates (16 states on 1 Jan 2027, +$0.26 to +$1.27) and FAR 52.222-43's 30-day notice (the timing anchor); SCA claim consultants (none found with public pricing — a second gap); PE facility-services roll-ups (267 NA transactions in 8 months of 2026; escalator realization is a named value lever) and Revomo (sells it to PE at $18k/yr+, contract module in alpha).
Sharpening pot (5 of 5): tested whether contractors really keep contracts as scattered PDFs and whether "contract administrator" roles track escalators (job postings confirm contract-admin and renewal duties but not escalator tracking specifically — so pain stayed at 8, not 9); searched Reddit/forums for missed-increase complaints in r/lawncare and r/Commercialcleaning (found spreadsheet-based agreement tracking in trade discussions but no smoking-gun complaint thread — this is why pain_type is expressed-but-quietly, and why the validation test reads real contracts rather than trusting forums); checked price-increase acceptance rates (no defensible benchmark — one undocumented 60-75% claim, logged as risk 2); checked PE demand for a contract-book audit at close (plausible and inferable from deal activity, not an established category — kept as the second buyer, not the first); and a final search for any existing escalator-tracker product for these trades returned essentially nothing, which is what held gap at 8.
Sharpening (7.2 to 8.1): Round 1 — weakest criterion: gap (6.5 before). Original shape was a generic "contract-to-billing revenue leakage auditor" for B2B SaaS finance teams. Research (Perplexity on revenue leakage; search on Tabs/Fazeshift/Nue/Subscript) showed that lane is crowded with funded quote-to-cash players and the leakage statistics are vendor-made and inconsistent (1-5% of revenue, 3-8% of ARR, 8.6% of contract value — all differently defined). So I moved the buyer away from SaaS finance entirely and onto recurring commercial-service contractors, where the systems of record (Aspire, ServiceTitan, BuildOps, ServiceTrade, Inspect Point) hold the agreement but, per their own docs and reviews, only do manual bulk percentage changes — no CPI clause interpretation, no notice-deadline enforcement. Found exactly one direct comparable, myhalo.ai, which is free-for-now, email-a-CSV, service-assisted and has no integration — strong evidence the problem is real and the product space is open. gap 6.5 → 8. pain also rose 7 → 8 once the compounding arithmetic and the near-100%-incremental-margin nature of the loss was made concrete.
Round 2 — weakest remaining: timing (7 before) and market_pull (6.5 before). Changed the idea to anchor on a dated forcing event rather than a general "AI reads documents" story: 16 states raise minimum wage on 1 Jan 2027 (+$0.26 NE to +$1.27 MI, EPI/Ballotpedia confirmed), which lands on the most labour-intensive contract books in the country and makes the change-in-law / wage pass-through clause the hot one; and on federal service work FAR 52.222-43 imposes a hard 30-day notice to claim the adjustment (eCFR confirmed). Also added the PE-platform buyer after confirming 267 North American facility-services M&A transactions in the first eight months of 2026 and that escalator realization is a recognised value-creation lever (Revomo sells exactly this to PE at $18k/yr + $18-36k per capability, with the contract module still in alpha). timing 7 → 8.5; market_pull 6.5 → 7.5 (held below 8 because I could not find a named role with a confirmed budget line for this specific purchase — contractors buy ops platforms, not pricing audits, and the clearest comparable in their own vertical is currently free). wedge 8 → 8.5 once I confirmed Halo's CSV-export motion works as a no-integration wedge.
What did not survive: I tried to anchor on a published rate of unapplied escalators and on a price-increase acceptance benchmark. Neither exists in any defensible form (one trade source claims 60-75% acceptance, undocumented). I therefore left pain at 8 rather than 9 and wrote both into riskiest_assumptions and the validation test instead of scoring them.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the Apple container 1.7.1 cluster docs (confirmed experimental local Kubernetes on Mac — real, but thin for a shareable project), the x.ai Grok Bot accounting post (five named bots owning order-to-cash, invoice processing 24h→minutes, humans retained for judgement — this became the cultural hook for the pick), and Claude Meetings (confirmed no public API, which killed candidate 7 outright).

Screening pot (5/5): one search each on agent fleet consoles (found paperclip, Cezar and a nine-tool orchestrator roundup — killed #3), code-smell/duplication tools (jscpd, super-linter — killed #4), transcript-to-whiteboard (Miro/FigJam/Claude artifacts — killed #7), job-title-to-bot-team tools (nothing direct, but it collided with the library's Roster — killed #2), and Apple container compatibility tooling (nothing to build on, weak audience — demoted #5).

Deep research pot (8/8): verified O*NET database licensing (CC BY 4.0, task statements and ratings bundleable into a static site); verified the Global Automation Atlas (18,797 tasks × 124 countries, Parquet/CSV, CC BY 4.0, but it already has its own public explorer — demoted #9); verified the "What Jobs Can AI Learn?" release including the exact file and column layout of RL-exposure-public (17,951 tasks, 894 occupations, D1-D8 dimensions, binding constraint, rl_index 0-100, three-model robustness, CC BY 4.0) — this is the backbone of the pick and the detail that let me specify the output precisely; searched for consumer "will AI take my job" tools and for a task-level equivalent (found none); and mapped the occupation-level prior art (jobs-exposure-atlas comparing Karpathy /jobs, OpenAI, Anthropic AEI, Microsoft Copilot, Bick et al., Frey-Osborne — publicly live, but occupation-level only and without the RL index). Net effect: the idea moved from occupation lookup to personal week log because the deep research proved the data is task-level.

Sharpening pot (4/4): confirmed Gravity Fast's "Can AI Do This Task?" is the nearest per-task competitor and lacks dataset, evidence or card; searched twice for any tool that scores a pasted personal task list or runs a weekly automatable-task leaderboard (no results both times, supporting freshness); and checked current cheap-model/embedding pricing to confirm the one tiny backend is affordable at launch traffic. The inverted "bottleneck" framing and the weekly trend strip both came out of this pot.
Sharpening (7.5 to 8.2): Round 1 — weakest criterion: usefulness (6.5). Original version was a one-shot "paste your job title, see your RL exposure" lookup — a toy you try once, and dangerously close to the occupation-level explorers that already exist. Change to the IDEA: move from occupation to the user's *own week*, stored per ISO week in localStorage, with a trend line of the "only you" share and a Friday refill prompt — it becomes a log of how your week shifts, not a quiz. Research (deep pot): confirmed the RL dataset is task-level (17,951 task statements with per-task binding constraint and 8 dimension scores), so a week of freeform lines can genuinely be scored line by line rather than rolled up — https://github.com/boukektkcl/RL-exposure-public. Also confirmed the only comparable explorers (jobs-exposure-atlas, aijobatlas) are occupation-level snapshots with no personal or repeat use. Usefulness 6.5 → 7.5; freshness held at 9 (May 2026 dataset, confirmed CC BY 4.0).

Round 2 — weakest criterion: shareability (7). The "x% of your job is automatable" card is a tired genre and reads as doom. Change to the IDEA: invert the hook — the headline output is the *bottleneck*, the named reason an agent cannot be trained on a given task ("nobody can grade this", "judgement is the job", "needs a real-world simulator"), with a "only you" percentage rather than a doom percentage. Research (sharpen pot): checked prior art for per-task tools — the closest is Gravity Fast's "Can AI Do This Task?", a single-task checker with an unexplained model guess and no dataset, card or week view (https://gravity.fast/tools/can-ai-do-this-task/); nothing surfaces a named binding constraint per task. Confirmed the dataset literally ships a binding-constraint and verification-bottleneck field per task, so the inverted framing is backed by data rather than invented. Shareability 7 → 8.5, wow 7.5 → 8. Did not raise buildability beyond 8: the freeform-line-to-O*NET-task match still needs one tiny embedding backend and is the real unknown.
prototype_summary: Escalator prototype: a drawer of 12 signed contract PDFs plus a stale spreadsheet transforms, in one click, into a dated dollar list of missed and upcoming price increases worth $34,114 unbilled, with clause evidence, shortfall maths, draft notice letters, a 3-year compounding gut-punch toggle, and a 12-month deadline calendar.
